title: Arabic, and translation
hook: Muslims hold the Qur'an to be the Arabic itself, and a translation to be its meanings

segments.voice: Yesterday, dots and vowels: marks added around the text so new readers could recite it rightly. Your line was marks for the reader. Did you leave one helpful mark for someone? Day three hundred nineteen.

Pick up an English Qur'an in a bookstore and look closely at the title page. Very often it doesn't simply say The Qur'an. It says something like The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, or The Meanings of the Qur'an in English. That isn't modesty for its own sake. It's a careful statement of what Muslims believe the book in your hands is, and what it isn't. Today: Arabic, and translation.
screen: `LOOK AT THE TITLE PAGE.` → `THE MEANING OF…` → `WHAT THE BOOK IS, AND ISN'T.`

segments.voice: Muslims hold that the Qur'an is the word of God in Arabic: not only its ideas, but its actual words, sounds and order. The Qur'an says so about itself more than once. In Pickthall's words: "Lo! We have revealed it, a Lecture in Arabic, that ye may understand." Lecture is Pickthall's old word for a reading, a recitation; the Arabic there is qur'an. So a translation, however good, is a human attempt to carry the meanings into another language. It's valuable, often essential, but Muslims don't call it the Qur'an itself. That's why Marmaduke Pickthall, whose English you've heard all year, called his 1930 work The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, and wrote in his foreword, in effect, that the Qur'an cannot be translated and his book was only an attempt to present its meaning. This shapes practice. The ritual prayer is said in Arabic wherever a Muslim lives, which is why children in Jakarta and Chicago learn al-Fatiha in the same sounds. Most scholars hold that a translation can't stand in for the Arabic in the prayer, while du'a, personal prayer, can be in any language. And it shapes how Muslims read. Arabic words often hold several layers at once. Rabb, in the Fatiha, is lord, but also the one who raises and nurtures. English has to choose, and every choice leaves something behind. So many Muslims read with a translation open beside the Arabic, and learn a little Arabic even if they never become fluent, to hear what the translation is pointing at. A translation is a meaning, and a meaning is a door. The Arabic is the house.
screen: `THE MEANING OF THE GLORIOUS KORAN` · `A LECTURE IN ARABIC` · `THE PRAYER IS SAID IN ARABIC` · `EVERY TRANSLATION CHOOSES`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a verse in two translations. After the bell, look up one short verse, al-Ikhlas is a good one, in two English translations, and notice where they choose different words. For now, sit with one Arabic word you know: bismillah, or alhamdulillah. Say it softly. Then say one English meaning of it. Then another. Notice how neither English quite fills the Arabic. Let the Arabic sit on its own for the last few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Arabic. The language Muslims hold the Qur'an was revealed in: the words themselves, not only their meaning. Today's word.

Your line: a translation is a meaning. Today, when you read or hear something translated, a verse, a song, a friend's message, ask what the original might hold that the translation had to leave behind. Day three hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Muslims recite the Qur'an in Arabic in prayer everywhere in the world, and read translations, often printed beside the Arabic, as translations of its meanings rather than as the Qur'an itself.

original.note: Arabic: Arabic. the Qur'an calls itself qur'anan 'arabiyyan, an Arabic recitation (12:2).

what a scholar hears: qur'anan 'arabiyyan in 12:2, and the classical discussion, with most scholars holding that the prayer must be recited in Arabic.
